old_catholic.papal_primacy:
Old Catholics can speak of papal primacy as a historical first place among the bishops of the ancient West, not as a power that rules the whole Church from Rome. In the undivided Church the bishop of Rome was often treated as primus inter pares, first among equals, whose voice carried weight in communion with the other apostolic sees. What we do not accept is the later claim that this primacy is a universal ordinary jurisdiction by which the pope may govern every local church as a matter of divine right.

After the First Vatican Council defined that kind of jurisdiction, communities that became Old Catholic held that such a definition went beyond the faith of the first centuries. Primacy, if it is to mean anything for us, is a ministry of communion and witness among sister churches, received in synodical life, not a monarchy over them. Local churches remain responsible for their own bishops and synods. Where Old Catholic bodies differ, it is usually over how far any honorary primacy of Rome could be recognised in a future reunion, not over whether Vatican I's jurisdictional primacy is binding.
old_catholic.papal_infallibility:
Old Catholic teaching is best named by its rejection of papal infallibility as defined in 1870. We do not hold that the bishop of Rome, speaking ex cathedra on faith or morals, is preserved from error by a personal charism that binds the whole Church without the consent of the episcopate and the faithful. Infallibility, so far as we use the word at all, belongs to the Church in her conciliar and lived consensus, not to one office acting apart from that consensus.

The Declaration of Utrecht stated that the Vatican decrees on the pope have no dogmatic force for us. That is not a denial that the Church can teach the apostolic faith with confidence; it is a denial that this confidence is located in a single see by divine constitution. Councils, Scripture as received in the ancient creeds, and the common tradition of East and West remain the measure. Individual Old Catholic churches may word the point more sharply or more irenically, but they agree that the 1870 definition is not part of the faith we confess.
